title: Pitch Type Classification with Random Forest
text:
Automated pitch classification models (such as MLB’s automated pitch tagging) use 3D kinematic tracking to predict the pitch type delivered by a pitcher. In this analysis, we train a multi-class Random Forest classifier via the tidymodels framework and the fast C++ ranger engine to predict six primary pitch types:

FF: Four-Seam Fastball
SI: Sinker / Two-Seam
SL: Slider
CH: Changeup
CU: Curveball
FC: Cutter

title: Pitch Type Classification with Random Forest
text:
Data Pipeline & Preprocessing
We query 25,000 right-handed pitches with complete physical parameters from the mlbr data lake via DuckDB:


Code
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  .libPaths(c("/mnt/storage/R/library", .libPaths()))
  library(mlbr)
  library(duckdb)
  library(dplyr)
  library(tidymodels)
  library(ranger)
  library(ggplot2)
})

con <- lake_duckdb()

df_pitches <- DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT 
    pitch_type,
    release_speed,
    release_spin_rate,
    pfx_x * 12.0 AS pfx_x_in,
    pfx_z * 12.0 AS pfx_z_in,
    vx0, vy0, vz0,
    ax, ay, az
  FROM statcast
  WHERE p_throws = 'R'
    AND pitch_type IN ('FF', 'SI', 'SL', 'CH', 'CU', 'FC')
    AND release_speed IS NOT NULL
    AND release_spin_rate IS NOT NULL
    AND pfx_x IS NOT NULL
    AND pfx_z IS NOT NULL
    AND vx0 IS NOT NULL
  USING SAMPLE 25000 (reservoir);
") %>%
  mutate(pitch_type = as.factor(pitch_type))

cat(sprintf("Prepared %d pitches for supervised classification.\n", nrow(df_pitches)))


Prepared 4098 pitches for supervised classification.

title: Pitch Type Classification with Random Forest
text:
Train / Test Splitting
We partition the dataset into an 80% training set and a 20% test holdout, stratified by pitch_type to preserve class proportions:


Code
set.seed(123)
pitch_split <- initial_split(df_pitches, prop = 0.80, strata = pitch_type)
train_data  <- training(pitch_split)
test_data   <- testing(pitch_split)

cat(sprintf("Training samples: %d | Test samples: %d\n", nrow(train_data), nrow(test_data)))


Training samples: 3276 | Test samples: 822

title: Pitch Type Classification with Random Forest
text:
Model Specification & Training
We specify a Random Forest classifier with 200 decision trees, capturing non-linear interactions between velocity, spin, and aerodynamic acceleration vectors:


Code
rf_spec <- rand_forest(trees = 200, mode = "classification") %>%
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity", num.threads = 8)

pitch_recipe <- recipe(pitch_type ~ ., data = train_data)

rf_workflow <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(pitch_recipe) %>%
  add_model(rf_spec)

# Fit workflow on training set
cat("Training Random Forest model on 8 threads...\n")


Training Random Forest model on 8 threads...


Code
rf_fit <- fit(rf_workflow, data = train_data)

title: Pitch Type Classification with Random Forest
text:
Test Evaluation & Metrics
We evaluate model predictions against the unseen holdout test set:


Code
test_preds <- predict(rf_fit, test_data) %>%
  bind_cols(predict(rf_fit, test_data, type = "prob")) %>%
  bind_cols(test_data %>% select(pitch_type))

# Compute Accuracy and Macro ROC-AUC
acc_res <- accuracy(test_preds, truth = pitch_type, estimate = .pred_class)
roc_res <- roc_auc(test_preds, truth = pitch_type, .pred_CH:.pred_SL)

metrics_df <- bind_rows(acc_res, roc_res)

This study adheres to the Q-CRISP protocol and the Medallion Full-Population Invariant: all pitch-level metrics are derived across the entire 14.64M-pitch Silver tier (v_statcast_features) without arbitrary subsampling, partitioned strictly into Discovery (2015–2023) and Out-of-Time Validation (2024–2026). title: Study 02: 4-Quadrant Platoon Physics & Situational Pitching Effectiveness
text:
1. Business & Scientific Understanding

1.1 Why Platoon Physics Drives Prediction Market Edge
Public sportsbooks and prediction markets (Kalshi, Polymarket) routinely anchor pitcher valuation on lagging, season-aggregate metrics such as ERA, FIP, or overall K%. Those aggregates implicitly average over a pitcher’s historical mix of left- and right-handed opponents.
In reality, a pitcher’s effectiveness is not a single scalar—it is a 4-quadrant physical interaction between release geometry, aerodynamic break vector, and batter swing plane: - Same-Hand Quadrants (RvR, LvL): Glove-side breaking pitches (ST, SL) sweep away from the batter’s barrel and visual depth plane. - Opposite-Hand Quadrants (RvL, LvR): That same glove-side pitch breaks into the batter’s swing path, forcing pitchers to rely on arm-side deception (CH, FS), vertical ride (FF), or steep drop (CU).
When an opposing manager stacks 6–7 opposite-handed hitters against a slider/sweeper-dependent starter, the pitcher’s true-talent strikeout rate and contact suppression degrade immediately—creating mispriced Over/Under totals, strikeout props, and moneylines.


1.2 Hypotheses

Hypothesis 2.1 (Batter-Perspective Break Symmetry): Platoon effectiveness is governed physically by horizontal break relative to the batter (hb_away_in), not pitcher handedness alone.
Hypothesis 2.2 (Multi-Metric Evaluation Invariant): Evaluating pitches on Whiff% alone systematically undervalues Sinkers (SI), which suppress xwOBA and drive positive RV/100 via ground balls (GB%) in same-hand matchups.
Hypothesis 2.3 (Platoon Vulnerability Index, PVI): Pitchers lacking an opposite-hand offspeed weapon (CH/FS) exhibit large PVI_csw and PVI_xwoba gaps and amplified 3rd-time-through-the-order (TTO) damage.

title: Study 02: 4-Quadrant Platoon Physics & Situational Pitching Effectiveness
text:
3. Mathematical Derivation: Symmetric Platoon Coordinates
To compare left- and right-handed pitchers on a unified geometric basis, Silver (v_statcast_features) defines two complementary horizontal break coordinates from Statcast pfx_x (hb_in = pfx_x * 12):

Pitcher-Perspective Horizontal Break (hb_glove_in): \[\text{hb\_glove\_in} = \text{hb\_in} \times \begin{cases} -1 & \text{if } \text{p\_throws} = \text{L} \\ +1 & \text{if } \text{p\_throws} = \text{R} \end{cases}\] Positive values always indicate glove-side break (ST, SL, FC); negative values always indicate arm-side run (SI, CH, FS).
Batter-Perspective Horizontal Break (hb_away_in): \[\text{hb\_away\_in} = \text{hb\_in} \times \begin{cases} -1 & \text{if } \text{stand} = \text{L} \\ +1 & \text{if } \text{stand} = \text{R} \end{cases}\] Positive values always break away from the batter; negative values always break in toward the batter.
Platoon Vulnerability Index (PVI): \[\text{PVI}_{\text{xwOBA}} = \text{xwOBA}_{\text{opp}} - \text{xwOBA}_{\text{same}}, \qquad \text{PVI}_{\text{CSW}} = \text{CSW\%}_{\text{same}} - \text{CSW\%}_{\text{opp}}\]

text:
6. Implementation & Reproducibility
All metrics in this study are pre-materialized in Silver (data/features/statcast_features/) and summarized into Gold Parquet tables (data/processed/platoon_quadrant_arsenal.parquet, data/processed/pitcher_pvi_2024_2026.parquet, data/processed/starter_tto_platoon_2020_2026.parquet).
library(mlbr)
con <- mlbr::lake_duckdb()

# Query any pitcher's 4-quadrant profile in ~40ms
DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT matchup, pitch_type, COUNT(*) AS n,
         ROUND(AVG(is_csw)*100, 1) AS csw_pct,
         ROUND(AVG(xwoba), 3) AS xwoba,
         ROUND(AVG(pitcher_run_exp)*100, 2) AS rv100
  FROM v_statcast_features
  WHERE game_year >= 2024 AND matchup IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY 1, 2
")

title: Non-Linear xwOBA & The Barrel Landscape
text:
In the Statcast era, a batter’s quality of contact is measured by two primary physical parameters: 1. Launch Speed (Exit Velocity, mph): How hard the ball leaves the bat. 2. Launch Angle (degrees): The vertical trajectory of the batted ball.
Traditional batting average and slugging percentage are heavily confounded by defense, ballpark dimensions, and random weather variation. Statcast’s Expected Weighted On-Base Average (xwOBA) and Expected Batting Average (xBA) remove these artifacts by modeling outcomes purely as a function of launch velocity and angle.
In this study, we train a 2D Generalized Additive Model (GAM) thin-plate spline to construct the continuous probability landscape of hits and visualize the famous Statcast “Barrel” zone.

title: Non-Linear xwOBA & The Barrel Landscape
text:
Data Extraction via DuckDB
We pull all fair batted ball events with valid exit velocity and launch angle metrics from the mlbr data lake:


Code
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  .libPaths(c("/mnt/storage/R/library", .libPaths()))
  library(mlbr)
  library(duckdb)
  library(dplyr)
  library(mgcv)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(viridis)
  library(scales)
})

con <- lake_duckdb()

# Sample 35,000 batted balls
batted_df <- DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT 
    events,
    launch_speed,
    launch_angle,
    CASE 
      WHEN events IN ('single', 'double', 'triple', 'home_run') THEN 1 
      ELSE 0 
    END AS is_hit,
    CASE 
      WHEN events = 'single' THEN 0.89
      WHEN events = 'double' THEN 1.27
      WHEN events = 'triple' THEN 1.62
      WHEN events = 'home_run' THEN 2.10
      ELSE 0.0
    END AS woba_val
  FROM statcast
  WHERE type = 'X'
    AND launch_speed BETWEEN 45 AND 120
    AND launch_angle BETWEEN -50 AND 80
    AND events IS NOT NULL
  USING SAMPLE 35000 (reservoir);
")

cat(sprintf("Loaded %d batted balls with complete exit velocity and launch angle.\n", nrow(batted_df)))


Loaded 1508 batted balls with complete exit velocity and launch angle.

title: Non-Linear xwOBA & The Barrel Landscape
text:
Fitting the 2D Thin-Plate Spline (GAM)
We fit a binomial GAM modeling hit probability:
\[\text{logit}(P(\text{Hit})) = s(\text{Launch Speed}, \text{Launch Angle})\]


Code
# Fit 2D thin-plate spline for hit probability
gam_hit <- gam(
  is_hit ~ s(launch_speed, launch_angle, k = 40),
  data = batted_df,
  family = binomial(link = "logit")
)

title: Non-Linear xwOBA & The Barrel Landscape

Generating the Probability Landscape Grid
We evaluate the fitted model over a dense 2D grid covering exit velocities from 50 to 115 mph and launch angles from -30° to 65°:


Code
grid <- expand.grid(
  launch_speed = seq(50, 115, length.out = 150),
  launch_angle = seq(-30, 65, length.out = 150)
)

  geom_tile(aes(fill = pred_hit_prob)) +

title: Non-Linear xwOBA & The Barrel Landscape
text:
Expected wOBA (xwOBA) Value Landscape
We fit a secondary Gaussian GAM to predict continuous wOBA run values:


Code
gam_woba <- gam(
  woba_val ~ s(launch_speed, launch_angle, k = 40),
  data = batted_df
)

grid$pred_woba <- predict(gam_woba, newdata = grid)
grid$pred_woba <- pmax(0, grid$pred_woba)

ggplot(grid, aes(x = launch_speed, y = launch_angle)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = pred_woba)) +
  scale_fill_viridis(
    option = "viridis",
    name = "Expected wOBA",
    limits = c(0, 1.8)
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    title = "Expected Run Value (xwOBA) Landscape",
    subtitle = "Peak run production (>1.500 wOBA) concentrates in the 100+ mph, 22°–32° corridor",
    x = "Exit Velocity (mph)",
    y = "Launch Angle (degrees)"
  ) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())















NoteKey Physical Takeaways




The Launch Angle Sweet Spot: Regardless of exit velocity, balls hit higher than 50° (popups) or lower than -10° (weak grounders) produce almost zero expected value.
Non-Linear Exit Velocity Returns: Below 90 mph, launch angle has modest effect on extra-base hits. Above 98 mph, each additional mph exponentially expands the allowable launch angle range for home runs.

title: The 24 Base-Out Run Expectancy Matrix (RE24)
text:
At any given moment in a baseball game, the state of the half-inning can be partitioned into 24 discrete base-out states: - 3 Out States: 0 outs, 1 out, 2 outs - 8 Base Occupancy States: Empty (___), 1st (1__), 2nd (_2_), 1st & 2nd (12_), 3rd (__3), 1st & 3rd (1_3), 2nd & 3rd (_23), and Bases Loaded (123).
Run Expectancy (RE) is the expected number of runs that will be scored from that point until the end of the half-inning. It forms the foundational bedrock of modern sabermetrics: \[\Delta \text{RE} = \text{RE}_{\text{state}_{t+1}} - \text{RE}_{\text{state}_t} + \text{Runs Scored on Play}\]
This difference (\(\Delta \text{RE}\)) is the empirical Run Value of any baseball event (single, strikeout, stolen base, double play), from which Linear Weights, wOBA constants, and WAR are derived.

title: The 24 Base-Out Run Expectancy Matrix (RE24)
text:
Extracting Plays via DuckDB
Using mlbr’s zero-copy DuckDB connection, we compute future half-inning runs directly over a sample of 150,000 modern regular season plays:


Code
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  .libPaths(c("/mnt/storage/R/library", .libPaths()))
  library(mlbr)
  library(duckdb)
  library(dplyr)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(tidyr)
  library(knitr)
  library(viridis)
})

con <- lake_duckdb()

# Compute base-out state and future inning runs using window functions
re24_raw <- DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "
  WITH play_events AS (
    SELECT 
      GAME_ID,
      TRY_CAST(INN_CT AS INTEGER) AS inn,
      BAT_HOME_ID,
      TRY_CAST(EVENT_ID AS INTEGER) AS event_id,
      TRY_CAST(OUTS_CT AS INTEGER) AS outs,
      CASE WHEN BASE1_RUN_ID != '' AND BASE1_RUN_ID IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END +
      CASE WHEN BASE2_RUN_ID != '' AND BASE2_RUN_ID IS NOT NULL THEN 2 ELSE 0 END +
      CASE WHEN BASE3_RUN_ID != '' AND BASE3_RUN_ID IS NOT NULL THEN 4 ELSE 0 END AS base_state,
      COALESCE(TRY_CAST(EVENT_RUNS_CT AS INTEGER), 0) AS runs_scored
    FROM retro_plays
    WHERE TRY_CAST(OUTS_CT AS INTEGER) BETWEEN 0 AND 2
      AND TRY_CAST(INN_CT AS INTEGER) BETWEEN 1 AND 9
    USING SAMPLE 150000 (reservoir)
  ),
  half_innings AS (
    SELECT 
      *,
      SUM(runs_scored) OVER (PARTITION BY GAME_ID, inn, BAT_HOME_ID) AS total_inn_runs,
      SUM(runs_scored) OVER (
        PARTITION BY GAME_ID, inn, BAT_HOME_ID 
        ORDER BY event_id 
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING
      ) AS runs_before
    FROM play_events
  )
  SELECT 
    outs,
    base_state,
    COALESCE(total_inn_runs - COALESCE(runs_before, 0), 0) AS rem_runs
  FROM half_innings
  WHERE outs BETWEEN 0 AND 2
    AND base_state BETWEEN 0 AND 7;
")

cat(sprintf("Extracted %d valid base-out state transitions.\n", nrow(re24_raw)))


Extracted 146719 valid base-out state transitions.

section: 1. The Physical Coordinate System of Modern Baseball
text:
1. The Physical Coordinate System of Modern Baseball
To understand how modern pitch models (like Stuff+ and Pitching+) work, you have to understand the 3D Cartesian coordinate system that Statcast and Hawkeye use to track every baseball.
                  +z (Vertical Height above ground)
                   |
                   |      Strike zone: ~1.5 ft to 3.5 ft
                   |
                   +------- +y (Mound is at y = 60.5 ft; Release is at y = 50 ft)
                  /
                 /
                /
             +x (Horizontal: Catcher's perspective)
                Negative = Batter's inside (for Righty)
                Positive = Batter's outside (for Righty)
                Center of plate = 0.0 ft

The Key Dimensions to Memorize:

\(y = 60.5\text{ ft}\): The pitching rubber.
\(y = 50.0\text{ ft}\): The standard Statcast tracking origin (\(v_{x0}, v_{y0}, v_{z0}\) are measured here). By 50 ft, the pitcher has released the ball and it is in pure aerodynamic flight.
\(y = 1.417\text{ ft}\): The front edge of home plate. Home plate is a 17-inch pentagon (\(17\text{ inches} / 12 = 1.4167\text{ ft}\)). This is where the pitch crosses the plate and where the bat makes contact.
\(y = 0.0\text{ ft}\): The back point of home plate (the origin).



Why Velocities and Accelerations Have Surprising Signs:

\(v_y\) is ALWAYS negative: Because the ball travels from the pitcher (\(y = 50\)) toward home plate (\(y = 0\)), its position in \(y\) is decreasing over time. A 95 mph fastball has a release velocity \(v_{y0} \approx -139\text{ ft/s}\).
\(a_y\) is positive: Air drag resists the baseball’s forward motion. Since the ball is moving in the negative \(y\) direction, drag pushes in the positive \(y\) direction (\(a_y \approx +25\) to \(+35\text{ ft/s}^2\)). This drag slows the ball down between the hand and the plate.

title: Lab 01 Work-Along: Aerodynamics, Trajectory Math & The Physics of Pitch Movement
text:
2. Hand-Calculating Trajectory Physics in R
In workbooks/lab01_aerodynamics_workbook.R, we begin with Part 1: hand-calculating real parameters from a 98.5 mph Four-Seam fastball.

Step 2.1: Terminal Forward Velocity at Home Plate
Using the classic kinematic equation \(v_f^2 = v_0^2 + 2 a \Delta y\):
\[\Delta y = 1.417 - 50.0 = -48.583\text{ ft}\] \[v_{y,f} = -\sqrt{v_{y0}^2 + 2 \cdot a_y \cdot (-48.583)}\]
vy0 <- -144.2   # ft/s (98.3 mph at 50 ft)
ay  <- 31.4     # ft/s^2 (forward air drag)
delta_y <- 1.417 - 50.0
vy_f <- -sqrt(vy0^2 + 2 * ay * delta_y) # -133.2 ft/s (90.8 mph at plate)
The pitch loses 7.5 mph of forward speed purely due to atmospheric air drag.


Step 2.2: Time of Flight
\[t_{\text{flight}} = \frac{v_{y,f} - v_{y0}}{a_y}\]
t_flight <- (vy_f - vy0) / ay # 0.3503 seconds (350 ms)
The batter has just 350 milliseconds from release to contact to recognize pitch type, predict trajectory, and execute the swing.


Step 2.3: Terminal Vertical & Horizontal Velocity
\[v_{z,f} = v_{z0} + a_z \cdot t_{\text{flight}}\] \[v_{x,f} = v_{x0} + a_x \cdot t_{\text{flight}}\]


Step 2.4: Approach Angles (VAA and HAA)
\[\text{VAA} = \arctan\left(\frac{v_{z,f}}{-v_{y,f}}\right) \times \left(\frac{180}{\pi}\right)\] \[\text{HAA} = \arctan\left(\frac{v_{x,f}}{-v_{y,f}}\right) \times \left(\frac{180}{\pi}\right)\]

section: 1. First-Principles Projection Math: Outs, Marcel & Uncertainty
text:
1. First-Principles Projection Math: Outs, Marcel & Uncertainty

Step 1.1: Never Treat Baseball Innings Pitched (.1/.2) as Decimals
FanGraphs and MLB box scores store 1 out as .1 and 2 outs as .2 (186.2 IP = 186.6667 decimal innings, NOT 186.20!). Always convert before sum-before-divide rate calculations:
\[\text{IP}_{\text{true}} = \lfloor \text{IP} \rfloor + \frac{\text{round}\big(10 \cdot (\text{IP} - \lfloor \text{IP} \rfloor)\big)}{3}\]


Step 1.2: Era-Adjusted Marcel Shrinkage & Tom Tango’s Age Factor
Recency weights \((w_1, w_2, w_3)\) (5/4/3 batters; 3/2/1 pitchers) pool multi-season excess skill above each season’s league average and regress toward the T-1 run environment using pre-backtest reliability denominator \(M_r\):
\[\hat{r}^{\text{Marcel}}_{i,T} = \mu_{\text{lg},T-1,g} + \frac{\sum_{k=1}^{3} w_k \, N_{i,T-k} \, (r_{i,T-k} - \mu_{\text{lg},T-k,g})}{\sum_{k=1}^{3} w_k \, N_{i,T-k} + M_r}\]
Running Part 1B demonstrates why sample-size shrinkage matters: - An established 27-year-old star (1,730 weighted PA across 3 years, .380/.365/.355 wOBA) earns 76.0% reliability weight → .355 regressed / .360 Tango-aged. - A hot 23-year-old rookie (180 PA, .380 wOBA) earns only 29.0% reliability weight → .332 regressed / .344 Tango-aged!


Step 1.3: Exposure-Calibrated 80% Uncertainty Bands
\[\text{CI}_{80\%}(i, T) = \hat{y}_{i,T} \pm 1.2816 \sqrt{\hat{\sigma}_{\text{skill}}^2 + \frac{\hat{\sigma}_{\text{noise}}^2}{\widehat{N}_{i,T}}}\]
As projected playing time grows from 150 → 350 → 600 PA, the 80% wOBA half-width tightens from ±.048 → ±.039 → ±.036 (hitting 82.8% pitcher FIP and 81.4% batter wOBA empirical coverage on locked 2025 OOS!).

Data lakes often degrade silently over time due to partial network failures, API rate limits, schema drift, or silent truncation. In baseball sabermetrics, a missing game or dropped column can invalidate WAR calculations, run expectancy matrices, and machine learning models.
mlbr provides a built-in verification suite (proof_lake()) that asserts 28 historical benchmarks, schema invariants, and physics boundaries across all 34+ million records.

Pedro Martinez 2000: Historic pitching peak (1.74 ERA, 284 Strikeouts, 0.737 WHIP).

Crosswalk Integrity:

Chadwick Bureau cross-mapping between MLBAM, Retrosheet, and Baseball-Reference achieves >99.5% match rate on modern players.

Statcast Physical & Coordinate Invariants:

Pitch release velocity strictly between 35 mph (slow eephus) and 107 mph (Aroldis Chapman record).
Release coordinates (release_pos_x, release_pos_z) within real-world physical pitcher release windows.
Zero requests hitting the silent 25,000 row truncation cap.

Retrosheet Game & Play Invariants:

Innings recorded have \(\le 3\) outs.
Base runner occupancy state values strictly within \(0 \le \text{state} \le 7\).
Score values strictly non-negative.

Schema Completeness:

0 columns dropped across all tables.

section: Universal ID Join Recipes for AI Agents
text:
Universal ID Join Recipes for AI Agents
AI agents should utilize these verified SQL templates to combine high-speed Statcast telemetry with historical player profiles and team schedules:

1. Statcast Telemetry \(\leftrightarrow\) Universal Player Names & IDs
SELECT 
  sc.game_date,
  sc.pitch_type,
  sc.release_speed,
  sc.plate_x,
  sc.plate_z,
  cw.name_first || ' ' || cw.name_last AS pitcher_name,
  cw.key_retro,
  cw.key_bbref,
  cw.key_fangraphs
FROM v_statcast sc
LEFT JOIN v_chadwick_register cw 
  ON sc.pitcher = cw.key_mlbam
WHERE sc.game_date >= '2024-01-01'
LIMIT 10;


2. Fast Whiff Rate by Pitch Type
SELECT 
  pitch_type,
  count(*) as total_pitches,
  round(avg(release_speed), 1) as avg_mph,
  round(avg(case when description in ('swinging_strike', 'swinging_strike_blocked', 'missed_bunt') then 1.0 else 0.0 end) * 100, 2) as whiff_pct
FROM v_statcast
WHERE pitch_type IS NOT NULL AND release_speed IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY pitch_type
HAVING count(*) > 50000
ORDER BY total_pitches DESC;


3. Bidirectional Game Crosswalk (Retrosheet \(\leftrightarrow\) Statcast)
library(mlbr)
# Retrosheet GAME_ID -> Statcast game_pk
crosswalk_game("BOS202304150", to = "game_pk")
# Returns: 718576

# Statcast game_pk -> Retrosheet GAME_ID
crosswalk_game(718576, to = "GAME_ID")
# Returns: "BOS202304150"

To equip external AI assistants (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, local Ollama) with complete knowledge of the mlbr data lake, copy the standardized prompt below:
You are an expert sabermetrician and DuckDB SQL analyst working with the `mlbr` baseball data lake.
- Canonical Lake: /mnt/storage/Rprojects/mlbr
- Access Engine: Zero-copy querying via DuckDB (con <- mlbr::lake_duckdb())
- Core Views:
  * v_statcast (14.64M raw pitches, 2008-2026, 119 metrics)
  * v_statcast_features (14.64M Silver pitches: VAA/HAA, hb_away_in, CSW/whiff/chase, xwOBA, ZSTD Parquet)
  * v_retrosheet_plays (~23.8M plays, 1900-2025, 160 fields)
  * v_retrosheet_games (123 seasons of game results)
  * v_chadwick_register (527k player ID crosswalks)
  * v_fangraphs_bat & v_fangraphs_pitch (1901-2025 WAR leaderboards)
  * v_mlbmeta_schedule (MLB schedules 2008-2026)

Rules:
1. Never run SELECT * on v_statcast or v_retrosheet_plays without filtering or aggregating.
2. Join Statcast players to Chadwick using: ON v_statcast.pitcher = v_chadwick_register.key_mlbam.
3. Bat speed and swing length are only available for 2024+ (NULL in earlier seasons).
4. The 2020 pandemic season contains 0 games between April and June.
5. Whiff & CSW definitions (Silver v_statcast_features): is_whiff = description IN ('swinging_strike', 'swinging_strike_blocked', 'foul_tip'); is_csw adds 'called_strike'.

title: Architecture & Storage
text:
Traditional sports analytics repositories suffer from two major anti-patterns: 1. Premature Aggregation / Column Dropping: Dropping columns during ingestion to save disk space, requiring full re-downloads when new research questions arise. 2. Monolithic Databases or Row-Oriented SQL Dumps: Storing 41.5M+ rows in .sql text dumps or single-writer database files (.duckdb, SQLite) creates file-lock contention, slow column scans, and tool lock-in.
mlbr resolves both by separating storage (ZSTD-compressed, key-sorted Apache Parquet) from query/compute (DuckDB SQL, R arrow, and Python pyarrow/polars).

mlbr resolves both by separating storage (ZSTD-compressed, key-sorted Apache Parquet) from query/compute (DuckDB SQL, R arrow, and Python pyarrow/polars).

ADR-001: Storage Format, Compression & SQL vs. Parquet

What Is sql/01_statcast_features.sql?
sql/01_statcast_features.sql is a DuckDB SQL view definition (CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_statcast_features ...), not a storage file. It stores zero data. Instead: - R/materialize_features.R executes the canonical view definition inside DuckDB and materializes the full 14.64M-row Silver table to ZSTD-compressed, key-sorted Parquet (data/features/statcast_features/). - mlbr::lake_register_features() mounts that Parquet dataset as v_statcast_features for sub-50ms SQL queries (falling back to live SQL evaluation over Bronze only when Silver isn’t materialized yet or force_dynamic = TRUE).

How Polars, Arrow & DuckDB Fit Together

In Memory (Zero-Copy Interchange): Polars uses Apache Arrow columnar buffers in memory (polars-arrow), the same memory layout used by DuckDB and R arrow via the Arrow C Data Interface. Moving query results between DuckDB SQL, R, and Python/Polars requires zero serialization copies.
On Disk (Canonical Storage): Polars and DuckDB both treat Apache Parquet as their primary analytical disk format. Combining COMPRESSION ZSTD with ROW_GROUP_SIZE = 100000 and ORDER BY (game_year, pitcher, game_date, game_pk, at_bat_number, pitch_number) shrinks the 14.64M-row Silver table from 1.6 GB (Snappy) down to 1.4 GB (ZSTD) while enabling Parquet min-max zone-map pruning (3.4× faster filtered reads).
Future Lakehouse Scaling (Delta Lake / Apache Iceberg): Because our canonical storage is already open Parquet, adding an Iceberg or Delta transaction log later requires zero data re-encoding if concurrent streaming writes grow.

section: 1. First-Principles Markov Pitch Pricing & Zero-Mean Decision VoE
text:
1. First-Principles Markov Pitch Pricing & Zero-Mean Decision VoE
Instead of regressing directly on noisy base-out delta_run_exp, Study 05 predicts 5 clean transition probabilities (p_sw, p_cs, p_wh, p_fl, xwOBA|BIP) and prices them via exact 2015–2023 context-neutral 12-count linear weights (\(\beta_{\text{xwOBA}} = 0.8593\)):
\[\text{EV}_{\text{take}} = \hat{p}_{\text{cs}}\,\Delta\text{RV}_{\text{strike}} + (1 - \hat{p}_{\text{cs}})\,\Delta\text{RV}_{\text{ball}}, \qquad \text{EV}_{\text{swing}} = \hat{p}_{\text{wh}}\,\Delta\text{RV}_{\text{strike}} + (1 - \hat{p}_{\text{wh}})\,\text{EV}_{\text{contact}}\] \[\text{decision\_voe}_i = (I_{\text{swing},i} - \hat{p}_{\text{sw},i})\big(\text{EV}_{\text{swing},i} - \text{EV}_{\text{take},i}\big)\]
Because we subtract the league-average swing probability \(\hat{p}_{\text{sw},i}\), an average batter’s expected decision_voe equals 0.000 identically across every pitch type and count—eliminating pitch-mix bias!
In Part 1 of workbooks/lab05_decomposed_pitching_decisions_workbook.R: - 3-2 Full-Count Chase Slider (p_sw = 0.45, p_cs = 0.05, p_wh = 0.52, xwOBA = .220): Taking earns a strong positive reward (EV_take >> EV_swing), while chasing incurs a steep run penalty because 3-2 has a 0.6018 run Ball-Strike spread! - 1-0 Heart-Zone Fastball (p_sw = 0.78, p_cs = 0.96, p_wh = 0.14, xwOBA = .460): Attacking generates positive run value (EV_swing > EV_take), whereas passively watching a strike costs expected runs.

title: Lab 03 Work-Along: Commit-Point Pitch Tunneling & Stuff+ / Location+
section: 1. Exact y₀ = 50 ft → 23.8 ft Commit-Point Tunneling Math
text:
1. Exact y₀ = 50 ft → 23.8 ft Commit-Point Tunneling Math
A batter must commit their swing roughly 175 ms before plate arrival, corresponding to \(y_{\text{commit}} = 23.8\text{ ft}\) from home plate (front edge \(y_{\text{plate}} = 1.417\text{ ft}\)). Because Statcast velocity/acceleration vectors (vx0, vy0, vz0, ax, ay, az) are anchored at \(y_0 = 50.0\text{ ft}\), we propagate each pitch forward from 50.0 ft using exact constant-acceleration kinematics:
\[\Delta y = y_{\text{target}} - 50.0, \qquad v_y(y_{\text{target}}) = -\sqrt{v_{y0}^2 + 2 a_y \Delta y}, \qquad t = \frac{v_y(y_{\text{target}}) - v_{y0}}{a_y}\] \[x(t) = x_0 + v_{x0} t + \tfrac{1}{2} a_x t^2, \qquad z(t) = z_0 + v_{z0} t + \tfrac{1}{2} a_z t^2\]
From sequential same-PA pitch pairs \((p_{k-1}, p_k)\) we compute Commit-Point Tunnel Separation (\(d_{\text{tunnel}}\) at 23.8 ft), Home-Plate Separation (\(d_{\text{plate}}\) at 1.417 ft), and the Pavlidis/Judge Break-to-Tunnel Ratio (BTR):
\[d_{\text{tunnel}} = 12 \sqrt{(x_k - x_{k-1})^2 + (z_k - z_{k-1})^2}\Big|_{y=23.8}, \qquad \text{BTR} = \frac{d_{\text{plate}}}{\max(d_{\text{tunnel}},\, 0.5\text{ in})}\]
In Part 1 of lab03_tunneling_stuff_plus_workbook.R, a 96 mph Four-Seamer (361.0 ms flight) followed by an 86 mph Gyro Slider (402.6 ms flight) separates by only 1.50 inches at the commit point (23.8 ft) before diverging to 9.93 inches at home plate — a 6.63× late-break tunnel ratio!

text:
1. Batter-Perspective Break Symmetry (hb_away_in) & PVI Math
Statcast measures horizontal break (pfx_x) from the catcher’s point of view (+ toward 1st base, - toward 3rd base). To compare all four handedness matchups (RvR, RvL, LvL, LvR) on a single physical axis, we define batter-perspective horizontal break away from the hitter:
\[\text{hb\_away\_in} = \begin{cases} +12 \cdot \text{pfx\_x} & \text{if } \text{stand} = \text{R} \text{ (1st-base side is away)} \\ -12 \cdot \text{pfx\_x} & \text{if } \text{stand} = \text{L} \text{ (3rd-base side is away)} \end{cases}\]
Under this coordinate transform, a 15-inch sweeper yields +15.0 in (breaking away from the barrel) in both RvR and LvL, and -15.0 in (breaking back into the barrel) in both RvL and LvR.

Empirical Bayes Pitcher Platoon Vulnerability Index (PVI)
Raw same-hand vs. opposite-hand splits are noisy for relievers and rookies. We stabilize each pitcher’s platoon split using the harmonic-mean effective sample size \(n_{\text{eff}}\) and shrinkage constant \(M = 800\) pitches:
\[n_{\text{eff}} = \frac{2 \, n_{\text{same}} \, n_{\text{opp}}}{n_{\text{same}} + n_{\text{opp}}}, \qquad \text{PVI}_{\text{xwOBA}} = \frac{n_{\text{eff}}}{n_{\text{eff}} + 800} \cdot (\text{xwOBA}_{\text{opp}} - \text{xwOBA}_{\text{same}})\]

A small sample (120 same vs. 120 opp, raw +0.080 split) receives only 13.0% weight → PVI = +0.010.
A large sample (1,800 same vs. 1,800 opp, raw +0.080 split) receives 69.2% weight → PVI = +0.055.

title: Study 01: Aerodynamics, Trajectory Physics & Approach Angles
text:
1. Business & Scientific Understanding

1.1 The Classical Evaluation Deficit
For decades, scouting and public sabermetrics evaluated pitchers primarily through two physical proxies: raw release velocity (\(v_{\text{release}}\)) and raw spin rate (\(\omega\)). While velocity correlates with swinging strike rate, these bulk variables consistently fail to explain why pitchers with identical velocity profiles exhibit vastly divergent whiff rates.
A prime example is the contrasting performance of fastballs with identical 95 mph release speed: - Pitcher A throws a 95 mph four-seamer that generates a 28% swing-and-miss rate. - Pitcher B throws a 95 mph four-seamer that generates a 12% swing-and-miss rate and is heavily punished on contact.
The missing physical mechanism lies in flight trajectory geometry: specifically, the angle at which the projectile traverses the strike zone relative to the batter’s plane of swing, known as the Vertical Approach Angle (VAA) and Horizontal Approach Angle (HAA).


1.2 The 5-Tier Hierarchical Predictive Architecture
Within the mlbr quantitative betting architecture, individual pitch dynamics constitute Level 1 (Pitch Physics & Quality). Level 1 models do not predict game winners directly; rather, they estimate the fundamental run-prevention and swing-inducing quality of every pitch thrown by a pitcher, conditioned on release geometry and trajectory mechanics.
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Level 5: Betting Market Edge & Kelly Staking (Polymarket / Kalshi)       |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                    ^

| Level 4: Game Simulation Engine (Monte Carlo Run-Expectancy Markov)      |

| Level 3: Team BaseRuns & Run-to-Win Translation                         |

| Level 1: Pitch Physics & Quality (Stuff+, Location+, Pitching+)         |
| -> Study 01 establishes the aerodynamic foundations for Level 1         |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+


1.3 Hypotheses

Hypothesis 1.1 (Trajectory Independence): Approach angles (VAA/HAA) provide orthogonal predictive information to raw velocity and induced vertical break (IVB).
Hypothesis 1.2 (Height-Conditional Whiff Lift): A four-seam fastball entering the top of the strike zone with a flatter VAA than physically expected for its height (\(\text{VAA}_{\text{diff}} > 0\)) produces a non-linear increase in swinging strikes due to batter perceptual motor error.

text:
3. Mathematical Derivation: Aerodynamic Trajectory Features

3.1 Terminal Velocity at the Strike Zone Plane
Statcast tracks the projectile’s trajectory from initial release (\(y_0 = 50.0\) ft from home plate) to the front edge of home plate (\(y_f = 1.417\) ft, or 17 inches) under constant acceleration assumptions: \[\vec{a}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} a_x \\ a_y \\ a_z \end{bmatrix}, \quad \vec{v}_0 = \begin{bmatrix} v_{x0} \\ v_{y0} \\ v_{z0} \end{bmatrix}\]
Using the kinematic equations under constant longitudinal drag \(a_y\): \[v_{yf}^2 = v_{y0}^2 + 2 a_y (y_f - 50.0)\]
Because the baseball moves toward home plate in a negative \(y\)-direction, \(v_{yf}\) is strictly negative: \[v_{yf} = -\sqrt{v_{y0}^2 + 2 a_y (1.417 - 50.0)}\]
The total time of flight \(t_{\text{flight}}\) from the 50-foot tracking point to plate contact is: \[t_{\text{flight}} = \frac{v_{yf} - v_{y0}}{a_y}\]
The terminal horizontal (\(v_{xf}\)) and vertical (\(v_{zf}\)) velocities at plate arrival are: \[v_{xf} = v_{x0} + a_x \cdot t_{\text{flight}}\] \[v_{zf} = v_{z0} + a_z \cdot t_{\text{flight}}\]


3.2 Vertical & Horizontal Approach Angles
The Vertical Approach Angle (VAA) is the angle in degrees between the velocity vector and the horizontal ground plane at the front of home plate: \[\text{VAA} = \text{atan2}(v_{zf}, -v_{yf}) \times \frac{180}{\pi}\]
The Horizontal Approach Angle (HAA) is the lateral approach angle relative to the straight line connecting the mound and home plate: \[\text{HAA} = \text{atan2}(v_{xf}, -v_{yf}) \times \frac{180}{\pi}\]


3.3 Platoon-Normalized Coordinates
Pitch location (plate_x) is defined from the umpire’s perspective (positive = catcher’s right / right-handed batter outside). To model pitch effectiveness invariant to batter handedness, we define Platoon-Normalized Plate X (plate_x_norm): \[\text{plate\_x\_norm} = \text{plate\_x} \times \begin{cases} -1.0 & \text{if batter stands Left (L)} \\ +1.0 & \text{if batter stands Right (R)} \end{cases}\] Under this transformation, positive values always represent pitches away / glove-side from the batter, and negative values represent inside / arm-side pitches.


3.4 Statcast Concentric Attack Zones
Following the MLB Statcast attack zone framework, every pitch is mapped into one of four concentric zones: - Heart: \(|\text{plate\_x}| \le 0.55\) ft and \(\text{plate\_z} \in [1.83, 3.17]\) ft. - Shadow: Edges of the strike zone (\(|\text{plate\_x}| \le 1.11\) ft and \(\text{plate\_z} \in [1.25, 3.75]\) ft), excluding Heart. - Chase: Expanded boundary (\(|\text{plate\_x}| \le 1.66\) ft and \(\text{plate\_z} \in [0.67, 4.33]\) ft), excluding Shadow. - Waste: All pitches completely outside the chase perimeter.


3.5 Expected VAA and VAA Difference (\(\text{VAA}_{\text{diff}}\))
Gravity dictates that pitches crossing the plate lower in the zone necessarily have steeper downward trajectories than pitches crossing high. To isolate the pitcher’s aerodynamic creation of flatness from mere location, we fit an empirical baseline for Four-Seam Fastballs: \[\mathbb{E}[\text{VAA} \mid \text{plate\_z}] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{plate\_z}\]
Empirical Ordinary Least Squares estimation over 1,000,901 modern fastballs yields: \[\mathbb{E}[\text{VAA}] = -7.71^\circ + 1.06 \cdot \text{plate\_z}\]
We then define the critical feature VAA Above Expected: \[\text{VAA}_{\text{diff}} = \text{VAA} - \mathbb{E}[\text{VAA} \mid \text{plate\_z}]\]

section: 5. Signal Evaluation: The Optical Mechanism of Whiff Lift
text:
5. Signal Evaluation: The Optical Mechanism of Whiff Lift

5.1 The “Rising Fastball” Optical Illusion
Human batters do not visually track the ball all the way into the catcher’s mitt. Instead, the batter’s neuromuscular system extrapolates the ball’s final trajectory based on sensory cues acquired during the first 150 milliseconds of flight.
When a pitcher delivers a fastball from a low release height with high backspin (high Induced Vertical Break), the pitch arrives at the top of the zone with \(\text{VAA}_{\text{diff}} > +1.5^\circ\) (flatter than expected). To the batter, the pitch appears to “rise” or carry through the hitting zone. The bat path, calibrated to an average descent angle of \(-5.5^\circ\), swings through the plane directly beneath the ball, producing a whiff.



Figure 2: Four-Seam Fastball Whiff Rate vs. VAA Above Expected




5.2 Quantitative Whiff Lift
As demonstrated in Figure 2: - Four-seamers with negative \(\text{VAA}_{\text{diff}}\) (steeper than expected, \(\le -1.5^\circ\)) generate whiff rates below 15%. - Neutral fastballs (\(\text{VAA}_{\text{diff}} \approx 0.0^\circ\)) generate baseline whiff rates of 21%. - Elite flat fastballs (\(\text{VAA}_{\text{diff}} \ge +2.0^\circ\)) produce whiff rates exceeding 32% on swings—a +52% relative increase in swing-and-miss efficiency without requiring additional velocity.

2. Domain Problem & Sabermetric Theory
Forecasting player talent is fundamentally a signal-to-noise extraction problem governed by four interacting mechanisms:

Finite-Sample Binomial & Contact Variance (Carleton Stabilization): A hitter’s K% reaches 50% true-talent reliability in ~50 PA, whereas BABIP, HR/9, and ERA require 500–900+ exposures. Using a single shrinkage denominator across all statistics under-regresses noisy outcomes and over-regresses fast-stabilizing skills.
Survivorship Bias vs. Zero-Sum League Conservation in Aging: Plotting cross-sectional mean wOBA or FIP by age makes 38-year-olds appear nearly identical to 27-year-olds because only elite outliers remain employed at 38. Conversely, applying uncentered within-player Delta-Method declines directly to a returning MLB cohort shifts the projected league average upward by +0.168 FIP because retiring veterans are replaced by incoming rookies. Tango’s Zero-Sum Conservation Law resolves both: estimate true biological slopes via midpoint harmonic-mean-weighted within-player pairs (with linear tail extrapolation past Age 39 so veteran decline remains strictly monotone), then zero-center the projected cohort’s exposure-weighted aging shift to conserve the T-1 league run environment.
Why xwOBA Alone Is Incomplete (Spray & Swing-Decision Blind Spots): Standard xwOBA depends solely on Exit Velocity and Launch Angle, ignoring horizontal spray angle. Pulled air balls (LA >= 10°, spray < -15° RHB / > +15° LHB — validated against FanGraphs Pull% at r = 0.932 overall and 0.962–0.977 within batter handedness) produce vastly higher wOBA than opposite-field fly balls (r = +0.203 with RHB wOBA - xwOBA — e.g., Isaac Paredes’s 39.1% raw 2025 Pulled Air% / 35.1% 3-year regressed prior drove a .352 observed wOBA over his .314 regressed xwOBA). Likewise, raw O-Swing% rewards overly passive hitters, whereas Zone-Chase Selectivity (Z-Swing% - O-Swing%, a SEAGER-inspired box-zone proxy) directly isolates pitch-recognition aggression (\(r_{\text{YoY}} = 0.800\)).
Preventing Sensor-Tier Over-Shrinkage via Stage-2 Residual Stacking: Newer Hawk-Eye sensors (mlbr Stuff+ OOS from 2024+, Hawk-Eye Bat Tracking from 2023+) have only 1 calibration season vs. 8–9 seasons for core Statcast metrics. Re-estimating 18 collinear predictors from scratch on \(N \approx 450\) pitchers with L2 cross-validation crushes the dynamic range (cal_slope = 1.8–2.2). Holding the multi-year M4_Statcast_Physics forecast fixed as a Stage-1 offset and learning a zero-mean Stage-2 Residual Ridge over the 3–4 orthogonal new sensor features preserves cal_slope ≈ 1.00 while cleanly capturing incremental physical lift.

3. Mathematical Formulation & Lake-Wide Pipeline

3.1 Exact Baseball Outs Conversion & July-1 Age Invariants
In v_fangraphs_pitch, IP is stored in baseball outs notation (.1 \(= 1/3\), .2 \(= 2/3\); verified 314–349 rows/season, 0 decimal rows). Every aggregation converts to exact decimal innings prior to sum-before-divide:
\[\text{IP}_{\text{true},i,s} = \lfloor \text{IP}_{i,s} \rfloor + \frac{\text{round}\big(10 \cdot (\text{IP}_{i,s} - \lfloor \text{IP}_{i,s} \rfloor)\big)}{3}, \qquad \text{Age}_{i,s} = s - \text{birth\_year}_i - \mathbb{I}(\text{birth\_month}_i \ge 7)\]
Verified 6,703 / 6,703 (100.00%) exact match between Chadwick birth dates and FanGraphs Age, and 3,687 / 3,687 (100.00%) join parity between v_fangraphs_pitch (TBF >= 50, 2020–2025) and Tier 1 Gold pitcher_stuff_plus.parquet.


3.2 Era-Adjusted Marcel, Midpoint Delta Aging & Component-Reconstructed FIP
For target season \(T\), role \(g \in \{\text{SP}, \text{RP}, \text{BAT}\}\), recency weights \((w_1, w_2, w_3)\) (5/4/3 batters; 3/2/1 pitchers), and pre-backtest (2006–2015) calibrated reliability denominators \(M_r\):
\[\hat{r}^{\text{Marcel}}_{i,T} = \mu_{\text{lg},T-1,g} + \frac{\sum_{k=1}^{3} w_k \, N_{i,T-k} \, (r_{i,T-k} - \mu_{\text{lg},T-k,g})}{\sum_{k=1}^{3} w_k \, N_{i,T-k} + M_r}\]
(2020 COVID-19 60-game season retains raw exposure \(N_{i,2020}\) in rate precision weighting while pro-rating playing-time inputs by \(162/60 = 2.70\times\). Baseline B2_Marcel_LinAge implements Tom Tango’s (2004) exact direct age multiplier \(m(a) = 1 + 0.006(29 - a)\) for \(a \le 29\) and \(1/(1 + 0.003(a - 29))\) for \(a > 29\), followed by Step 6 projected-exposure league rebaselining.)
Consecutive same-player, same-role pairs \((s-1, s)\) with \(s \in [2003, T-1]\) estimate smooth midpoint (age_mid = age - 0.5) harmonic-mean-weighted Delta-Method curves \(\hat{\delta}_g(a)\) with inverse-variance weights \(W_{i,a}^{\text{harm}} = \frac{2 N_{i,s-1} N_{i,s}}{N_{i,s-1} + N_{i,s}}\) and linear marginal-slope extrapolation beyond [21, 39] (preventing endpoint clamping artifacts at Age 40+). Integrating from weighted historical age \(\bar{a}_{i,T}\) to target age \(a_{i,T}\) and applying Tango’s zero-sum normalization yields B3:
\[\Delta^{\text{raw}}_{\text{age}}(i, T) = \int_{\bar{a}_{i,T}}^{a_{i,T}} \hat{\delta}_g(u)\,du, \qquad \Delta^{\text{norm}}_{\text{age}}(i, T) = \Delta^{\text{raw}}_{\text{age}}(i, T) - \frac{\sum_{j \in g} \widehat{N}_{j,T}\,\Delta^{\text{raw}}_{\text{age}}(j, T)}{\sum_{j \in g} \widehat{N}_{j,T}}\]


3.3 Stage-1 Expanding Physics Ridge, Stage-2 Sensor Residual Stacking & Uncertainty Bands

Stage-1 Expanding Statcast Physics (M4_Statcast_Physics): Season-grouped L2 Ridge (glmnet, \(\alpha=0\)) trained strictly on target seasons 2016 .. T-1 (0 imputed cells across all folds) over B3 rates plus regressed Statcast physics (SwStr%, CSW%, FBv, delta_fbv, GB%, HardHit%, Barrel%, xERA, pulled_air_allowed_pct, strictly seasonal pooled sum-before-shrink PVI_xwoba/PVI_csw for pitchers; xwOBA, xwOBA - wOBA, Barrel%, HardHit%, EV90, pulled_air_pct, sweet_spot_pct, O-Swing%, Z-Contact%, SwStr%, zone_chase_selectivity for batters).
Stage-2 Residual Sensor Stack (M4_mlbr_StuffPlus, M4_BatTracking): Holds Stage-1 fixed as an offset and fits a compact zero-mean residual Ridge on 2023 → 2024 (2024 100% unseen by Study 03’s 2015–2023 XGBoost training) over the 3–4 orthogonal new sensor variables (stuff_plus_t1, loc_plus_t1, pitch_plus_t1, tunnel_plus_t1 or batspeed_t1, blast_t1, sq_swing_t1, swing_len_t1).
Component-Reconstructed FIP (M4_Component_FIP): Synthesizes projected K%, BB%, HR/9, regressed HBP%, role TBF/IP, and prior-year \(c\text{FIP}_{T-1}\) into an internally consistent run-prevention forecast.
Exposure-Calibrated 80% Uncertainty Bands: Regressing pre-2025 OOS squared residuals \(e_i^2\) on \(1/N_i\) decomposes uncertainty into irreducible talent variance + exposure noise:

\[\text{CI}_{80\%}(i, T) = \hat{y}_{i,T} \pm 1.2816 \sqrt{\hat{\sigma}_{\text{skill}}^2 + \frac{\hat{\sigma}_{\text{noise}}^2}{\widehat{N}_{i,T}}}\]

title: Study 03: Commit-Point Pitch Tunneling & Platoon-Conditioned Stuff+ / Pitching+
text:
2. Domain Problem & Theoretical Physics

2.1 Perceptual Commit-Point Mechanics (Pavlidis & Judge, 2017)
A 95 mph fastball travels from release (~54.5 ft) to home plate (1.417 ft) in roughly 390 ms. Because human visual processing requires ~150 ms and bat swing initiation/execution requires another ~150 ms, hitters must commit to swinging when the ball is roughly 167 ms from home plate — corresponding spatially to the commit plane at \(y_{\text{commit}} = 23.8\text{ ft}\).
Pitch deception operates in two consecutive spatial stages: 1. Pre-Commit Masking (Small tunnel_dist_in): Pitch \(N\) travels down nearly the identical 3D corridor as Pitch \(N-1\) up to \(y = 23.8\text{ ft}\), preventing early pitch recognition. 2. Post-Commit Divergence (Large post_tunnel_break_in): After the hitter commits to a swing plane, Magnus and seam-shifted wake forces bend Pitch \(N\) away from Pitch \(N-1\)’s trajectory, maximizing Pavlidis & Judge’s Break-to-Tunnel Ratio (post_tunnel_break_in / max(tunnel_dist_in, 1.0)).


2.2 Why Linear Models & Naive Release Shortcuts Fail

Coordinate Frame Trap: Statcast’s 9-parameter constant-acceleration kinematics \((v_{x0}, v_{y0}, v_{z0}, a_x, a_y, a_z)\) are defined strictly at \(y_0 = 50.0\text{ ft}\), whereas (release_pos_x, release_pos_z) are reported at release_pos_y (\(\approx 54.5\text{ ft}\)). Integrating forward from release_pos_x using \(t_{\text{dec}}\) omits ~4.5 ft of flight and introduces a 2.87-inch mean (4.69-inch p95) coordinate error at \(y = 23.8\text{ ft}\).
Non-Linearity of Pitch Value: A glove-side slider is devastating on the outer shadow against a same-hand hitter (0-2 count) but crushed in the heart of the zone against an opposite-hand hitter (2-0 count). Analytical Ridge models average away count × location × platoon interactions (0.028% out-of-sample \(R^2\)), whereas xgboost leaps to 3.777%.
Orthogonal Stuff+ vs. Location+ Decomposition (Sarris, Bay, Grove): Separating physical stuff (Stuff+), pure count-and-zone command (Location+), and combined execution (Pitching+) isolates two independent pitcher skills (r = -0.034): Stuff+ governs Strikeout Rate (K%), while Location+ governs Walk Avoidance (BB%).

title: Study 03: Commit-Point Pitch Tunneling & Platoon-Conditioned Stuff+ / Pitching+
text:
3. Mathematical Formulation & Lake-Wide Pipeline

3.1 Exact \(y_0 = 50\text{ ft}\) Commit-Point Reconstruction
Given terminal flight time \(t_p\) from \(y_0 = 50.0\text{ ft}\) to the front edge of home plate (\(y_p = 1.417\text{ ft}\)) and commit-point flight time \(t_{\text{dec}}\) to \(y_{\text{commit}} = 23.8\text{ ft}\):
\[t_p = \frac{-\sqrt{v_{y0}^2 + 2 a_y (1.417 - 50.0)} - v_{y0}}{a_y}, \qquad t_{\text{dec}} = \frac{-\sqrt{v_{y0}^2 + 2 a_y (23.8 - 50.0)} - v_{y0}}{a_y}\]
We reconstruct the exact 3D coordinates at \(y_0 = 50.0\text{ ft}\) from observed (plate_x, plate_z) and integrate forward to \(y_{\text{commit}} = 23.8\text{ ft}\) (empirically verified to close back to observed (release_pos_x, release_pos_z) at release_pos_y within 0.046 in mean error across 100,000 Hawk-Eye pitches):
\[x_{50} = \text{plate\_x} - v_{x0} t_p - \frac{1}{2} a_x t_p^2, \qquad z_{50} = \text{plate\_z} - v_{z0} t_p - \frac{1}{2} a_z t_p^2\]
\[x_{\text{dec}} = x_{50} + v_{x0} t_{\text{dec}} + \frac{1}{2} a_x t_{\text{dec}}^2, \qquad z_{\text{dec}} = z_{50} + v_{z0} t_{\text{dec}} + \frac{1}{2} a_z t_{\text{dec}}^2\]
For consecutive pitches (\(N-1 \to N\)) thrown by the same pitcher (prev_pitcher = pitcher) with zero skipped pitch numbers (prev_pitch_number = pitch_number - 1):
\[d_{\text{tunnel}} = 12 \sqrt{(x_{\text{dec}, N} - x_{\text{dec}, N-1})^2 + (z_{\text{dec}, N} - z_{\text{dec}, N-1})^2}\text{ (in)}\]
\[d_{\text{post}} = 12 \sqrt{\bigl((\text{plate\_x}_N - x_{\text{dec}, N}) - (\text{plate\_x}_{N-1} - x_{\text{dec}, N-1})\bigr)^2 + \bigl((\text{plate\_z}_N - z_{\text{dec}, N}) - (\text{plate\_z}_{N-1} - z_{\text{dec}, N-1})\bigr)^2}\text{ (in)}\]
\[\text{Break-to-Tunnel Ratio (BP)} = \frac{d_{\text{post}}}{\max(d_{\text{tunnel}}, 1.0)}, \qquad \text{Plate-to-Tunnel Ratio} = \frac{d_{\text{plate}}}{\max(d_{\text{tunnel}}, 1.0)}\]


3.2 Silver Materialization (v_statcast_tunneling, ADR-001 Strictly Verified)
Executed across all 19 Statcast seasons (2008–2026, preserving all game types per ADR-002 with game_type exposed for zero-copy filtering) by R/materialize_tunneling.R reading canonical sql/02_pitch_tunneling.sql: - Total consecutive pairs materialized: 10,201,496 (2008-03-28 to 2026-10-28) - Integrity & sensor guards: Requires ay > 1e-6, vy0 < -40, plate_x ∈ [-10, 10], plate_z ∈ [-10, 15], t_flight ∈ [0.15, 1.2], and non-null pitch_type/release_speed/kinematics — yielding bad_rows = 0 and dup_groups = 0 on (game_pk, at_bat_number, pitch_number). - Verified ADR-001 sort order: Single-threaded per-year sorted Parquet writes (ROW_GROUP_SIZE = 100000, ZSTD, Hive game_year) verified across all 19 seasons with 0 pitcher sort inversions, 0 row-group min-max overlaps, and 15.0 ms single-pitcher pruned query latency!


3.3 Leak-Free Fastball Anchors & 2024 Out-of-Sample Plus-Scale Lock
Per-pitcher within-season fastball anchors (FF, SI, FC) use strictly prior regular-season pitches (ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING). Plus-scale calibration locks \((\mu_{2024}, \sigma_{\text{pit}, 2024})\) strictly on 2024 Regular-Season out-of-sample predictions (across pitchers with \(\ge 250\) pitches), leaving 2025–2026 100% untouched:
\[\text{Score+}_{i, m} = 100 + 10 \cdot \frac{\hat{r}_{i, m} - \mu_{2024, m}}{\sigma_{\text{pit}, 2024, m}}\]

text:
2. Domain Problem & Sabermetric Theory
Why did Study 03’s single-head delta_run_exp model leave signal on the table — and how does fixing it simultaneously unlock pitch-level batter evaluation?

Base-Out State Contamination in Raw delta_run_exp: A 3-2 ball with the bases loaded and 2 outs carries -0.85 pitcher runs, whereas the exact same pitch with bases empty carries -0.29 runs. Training an L2 loss tree ensemble on raw delta_run_exp gives high-leverage innings ~8× squared-error weight and mixes situational context into pitch-quality splits.
Non-Linearity of Pitch Outcomes: Different physical mechanisms govern different sub-events:

p(called strike | take) depends sharply on plate_x_norm, sz_norm_z, count, and late break (0.1486 logloss!).
p(whiff | swing) depends heavily on velocity, VAA/IVB, and commit-point tunneling (v_statcast_tunneling).
E[xwOBA | BIP] depends on pitch location, velocity/movement, and launch-angle suppression. Fitting dedicated logloss / RMSE heads to each physical transition prevents high-variance batted balls from drowning out sharp strike-zone and whiff boundaries.

Why Pitch-Level Zero-Mean Decision Value (Decision+) Beats Z-O%: Study 04’s Zone-Chase (Z-O%) treats every pitch inside the rulebook strike zone identically (+1) and every pitch outside identically (-1). In reality, swinging at a 3-0 fastball on the black is far less valuable than swinging at a 1-0 heart-zone meatball, and chasing a 3-2 slider (0.6018 run Ball-Strike spread!) is 8× costlier than chasing on 0-0 (0.0750 spread). Pricing each pitch’s exact \((\text{EV}_{\text{swing}} - \text{EV}_{\text{take}})\) and subtracting the league-average swing probability \(\hat{p}_{\text{sw}}\) yields a strictly zero-mean, pitch-mix-unbiased SEAGER-class metric.

title: Study 05: Context-Neutral Decomposed Pitching+ & Pitch-Level Batter Process Engine
text:
3. Mathematical Formulation & Zero-Leakage Architecture

3.1 Context-Neutral 12-Count Linear Weights & BIP xwOBA → RV Map (2015–2023 Train Only)
Strictly on 2015–2023 Regular-Season pitches (5,972,773 rows, zero 2024–2026 data), we compute empirical batter-perspective transition values for each count \((b, s) \in \{0..3\} \times \{0..2\}\): - \(\Delta\text{RV}_{\text{ball}}(b,s)\), \(\Delta\text{RV}_{\text{strike}}(b,s)\), and \(\Delta\text{RV}_{\text{foul}}(b,s)\) (= 0.0000 identically when \(s = 2\)). - For balls in play (> 900K training BIPs with finite xwoba), OLS fits \(\Delta\text{RV}_{\text{BIP}}(b,s,\widehat{\text{xwOBA}}) = \alpha_{b,s} + \beta \cdot \widehat{\text{xwOBA}}\), yielding \(\beta = 0.8593\) (\(R^2 = 0.4472\), matching theoretical \(1 / w_{\text{scale}} \approx 0.86\) to three decimals!).


3.2 Five-Head Decomposed Expected Value & Martingale Count Centering
Given 5 chronological xgboost heads (\(\hat{p}_{\text{sw}}, \hat{p}_{\text{cs}}, \hat{p}_{\text{wh}}, \hat{p}_{\text{fl}}, \widehat{\text{xwOBA}}\)):
\[\text{EV}_{\text{take},i} = \hat{p}_{\text{cs},i}\,\Delta\text{RV}_{\text{strike}}(b_i,s_i) + (1 - \hat{p}_{\text{cs},i})\,\Delta\text{RV}_{\text{ball}}(b_i,s_i)\] \[\text{EV}_{\text{contact},i} = \hat{p}_{\text{fl},i}\,\Delta\text{RV}_{\text{foul}}(b_i,s_i) + (1 - \hat{p}_{\text{fl},i})\big(\alpha_{b_i,s_i} + 0.8593\,\widehat{\text{xwOBA}}_i\big)\] \[\text{EV}_{\text{swing},i} = \hat{p}_{\text{wh},i}\,\Delta\text{RV}_{\text{strike}}(b_i,s_i) + (1 - \hat{p}_{\text{wh},i})\,\text{EV}_{\text{contact},i}\] \[\widehat{\text{xRV}}_{\text{bat},i} = (1 - \hat{p}_{\text{sw},i})\,\text{EV}_{\text{take},i} + \hat{p}_{\text{sw},i}\,\text{EV}_{\text{swing},i}\]

Count-Free Decomp Stuff+: Priced with marginal count-frequency-weighted linear weights (rv_ball = +0.0665, rv_strike = -0.1026), guaranteeing zero count or location leakage.
Martingale Count-Centered Location+ / Pitching+ / Pitching+Tunnel: Subtracting the 2020–2023 training mean within each count cell ensures \(\mathbb{E}[\text{xRV}_{\text{centered}} \mid b, s] \equiv 0\), so pitchers are graded purely on execution within each count.



3.3 Exact Additive Pitch-Level Batter Process Decomposition
Using the locked full-context Decomp Pitching+Tunnel probability surface:
\[\text{decision\_voe}_i = (I_{\text{swing},i} - \hat{p}_{\text{sw},i})\big(\text{EV}_{\text{swing},i} - \text{EV}_{\text{take},i}\big)\] \[\text{bat\_ctrl\_rv}_i = I_{\text{swing},i}\,(\hat{p}_{\text{wh},i} - I_{\text{whiff},i})\big(\text{EV}_{\text{contact},i} - \Delta\text{RV}_{\text{strike}}(b_i,s_i)\big)\] \[\text{contact\_rv}_i = I_{\text{bip},i} \cdot 0.8593 \cdot (\text{xwOBA}_i - \widehat{\text{xwOBA}}_i)\] \[\text{process\_rv}_i = \text{decision\_voe}_i + \text{bat\_ctrl\_rv}_i + \text{contact\_rv}_i\]
All season rates use sum-before-divide (rv100 = 100 * sum(rv) / n_pitches) and standardize to 100 ± 10 strictly on 2024 qualified cohorts (>= 500 pitches thrown; >= 1,000 pitches seen).

title: Unsupervised Pitch Clustering with K-Means
text:
In Major League Baseball, pitch types are traditionally labeled by human operators or proprietary MLBAM heuristic algorithms (e.g., Four-Seam Fastball FF, Slider SL, Changeup CH, Curveball CU). However, pitch design exists on a continuous physical continuum: hybrid pitches like “sweepers”, “hard cutters”, and “slurves” often defy discrete classification.
In this analysis, we use unsupervised clustering (K-Means) over raw Statcast flight physics to discover natural pitch movement profiles directly from empirical data.

title: Unsupervised Pitch Clustering with K-Means
text:
Feature Scaling & Optimal \(k\) Selection
Because release speed (~90 mph) and spin rate (~2200 rpm) have much larger numerical scales than break measurements (~10 inches), we standardize features using Z-score scaling (\(z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\)).
We then evaluate within-cluster sum of squares (WSS) across \(k \in \{2, \dots, 8\}\) using the Elbow Method:


Code
# Standardize features
features <- pitches_raw %>%
  select(release_speed, release_spin_rate, pfx_x_in, pfx_z_in) %>%
  scale()

# Compute total within-cluster sum of squares
set.seed(42)
k_values <- 2:8
wss <- numeric(length(k_values))

for (i in seq_along(k_values)) {
  km_fit <- kmeans(features, centers = k_values[i], nstart = 10, iter.max = 50)
  wss[i] <- km_fit$tot.withinss
}

elbow_df <- data.frame(k = k_values, wss = wss)

ggplot(elbow_df, aes(x = k, y = wss)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2b5c8f", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(color = "#f37626", size = 3.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 4, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "K-Means Elbow Method for Optimal Pitch Clusters",
    subtitle = "Distinct inflection point observed around k = 4 (Fastballs, Breaking Balls, Offspeed, Cutters)",
    x = "Number of Clusters (k)",
    y = "Total Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WSS)"
  )

title: Unsupervised Pitch Clustering with K-Means
text:
Fitting K-Means (\(k = 4\))
We fit our final model with \(k = 4\) clusters, representing the 4 primary pitch movement archetypes:


Code
set.seed(42)
km_final <- kmeans(features, centers = 4, nstart = 25, iter.max = 100)
pitches_raw$cluster <- as.factor(km_final$cluster)

# Calculate cluster profile means
cluster_profiles <- pitches_raw %>%
  group_by(cluster) %>%
  summarize(
    count = n(),
    avg_velocity = mean(release_speed),
    avg_spin = mean(release_spin_rate),
    avg_hbreak = mean(pfx_x_in),
    avg_vbreak = mean(pfx_z_in)
  )
